```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3
)
```

`tidygenclust` estimates ancestry with the ADMIXTURE model natively, with
`gt_radmix()`. It also provides interfaces to three external programs that
fit the same model: the original ADMIXTURE program (Alexander et al. 2009),
run with `tidypopgen::gt_admixture()`, and the python packages fastmixture
(Santander et al. 2024), run with `gt_fastmixture()`, and ADAMIXTURE
(Saurina-i-Ricos et al. 2026), run with `gt_adamixture()`. These programs
are optional: they are not needed by the rest of `tidygenclust`.

In this article, we show how to install the three programs and how to run
them, alongside `gt_radmix()`, on the dataset of the lizard *Anolis
punctatus* (Prates et al. 2018) used in the main vignette, and we check that
the four programs give consistent ancestry proportions. For a comparison
of their performance, see the article "Benchmarking gt_radmix() against
ADMIXTURE, fastmixture and ADAMIXTURE".

`gt_radmix()` estimates individual ancestry proportions (Q) and ancestral
allele frequencies (P) with the method of ADMIXTURE, using a modified
version of the algorithm of OpenADMIXTURE (Ko et al. 2023). Much of its C++
code is ported from the Julia implementation of OpenADMIXTURE,
OpenADMIXTURE.jl, so no Julia or Python is needed. It differs from
OpenADMIXTURE, hence its different name: it does not include the selection
of ancestry informative markers; we implemented the cross-validation of
ADMIXTURE, to choose K, which is not part of OpenADMIXTURE; it supports
pseudohaploid data; and it changes some details of the computations (see
`?gt_radmix`). If you use it, please cite Ko et al. (2023) for the
algorithm, as well as Alexander et al. (2009) for the method. If you use
fastmixture, cite Santander et al. (2024), if you use ADAMIXTURE,
Saurina-i-Ricos et al. (2026), and if you use ADMIXTURE, Alexander et al.
(2009).

# Installing the external tools

We use `reticulate` to install the three programs in a conda environment
(`ctidygenclust`; on macOS, ADMIXTURE is installed in an environment of its
own, `cadmixture86`), so you, as a user, should not need to worry about the
details of the python packages or their dependencies. This works on Linux
and macOS, but NOT on Windows (where you can use the WSL). ADAMIXTURE is
installed from PyPI in its CPU version, which does not need PyTorch. You can
install all three programs with:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(tidygenclust)
tgc_tools_install()
```

or choose which programs to install, e.g. only `fastmixture`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tgc_tools_install(tools = "fastmixture")
```

Programs can be added later to an existing environment with
`tgc_fastmixture_install()`, `tgc_admixture_install()` and
`tgc_adamixture_install()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tgc_admixture_install()
```

## For macOS users

If you want to install `fastmixture` or ADAMIXTURE, which are compiled from
source on macOS (so that they use the same OpenMP library), you need `llvm`
and `libomp` installed via `brew` in the first place. In `bash`, you will
need:

``` bash
# llvm can be installed via brew
brew install llvm libomp
```

## Checking which programs are installed

`tgc_tools_version()` reports which programs are installed (`NA` for those
that are not):

```{r}
library(tidypopgen)
library(tidygenclust)

tools_version <- tgc_tools_version()
tools_version
```

The code that runs each program in this article is only run if that
program is available, and the comparison only if all three are:

```{r}
fastmixture_available <- !is.na(tools_version$fastmixture)
admixture_available <- !is.na(tools_version$admixture)
adamixture_available <- !is.na(tools_version$adamixture)
all_available <- fastmixture_available && admixture_available &&
  adamixture_available
```

# The data

We read the vcf file of the 46 lizards into a `gen_tibble`, add the
population information, and group the individuals by the three genetic
groups found by Prates et al. (2018): Eastern Amazonia (Eam), Western
Amazonia (Wam) and the Atlantic Forest (AF):

```{r}
vcf_path <- system.file(
  "/extdata/anolis/punctatus_t70_s10_n46_filtered.recode.vcf.gz",
  package = "tidypopgen"
)
anole_gt <- gen_tibble(vcf_path,
  quiet = TRUE, backingfile = tempfile("anolis_"),
  parser = "cpp"
)
pops_path <- system.file("/extdata/anolis/punctatus_n46_meta.csv",
  package = "tidypopgen"
)
pops <- utils::read.csv(pops_path)
anole_gt <- anole_gt %>%
  left_join(pops, by = "id") %>%
  group_by(pop)
anole_gt
```

For each program, we make a single run for K = 3.

# Running gt_radmix()

```{r}
anole_radmix <- gt_radmix(anole_gt, k = 3, seed = 1)
summary(anole_radmix)
```

The results are stored in a `gt_admix` object, so we can use all the methods
from `tidypopgen` (see the main vignette).

# Running fastmixture

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = fastmixture_available)
```

`gt_fastmixture()` runs fastmixture on a `gen_tibble` (reading its backing
file directly) or on a set of PLINK files. Its arguments follow those of
fastmixture, so some differ from those of `gt_radmix()`: the number of
cores is set with `threads`, and cross-validation with `cv`, the number of
folds. By default, it only returns the Q matrices (set `no_freqs = FALSE`
to also keep the P matrices). As the fastmixture program does, it starts
from a randomised SVD of the genotypes, which needs all the loci to be
polymorphic (`random_init = TRUE` starts from random values instead, but
can take much longer to converge). fastmixture prints its progress, which
we hide here:

```{r, results = "hide"}
anole_fm <- gt_fastmixture(anole_gt, k = 3, seed = 1)
```

```{r}
summary(anole_fm)
```

# Running ADMIXTURE

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = admixture_available)
```

`tidypopgen::gt_admixture()` runs the original ADMIXTURE program: it writes
the `gen_tibble` to PLINK files, runs ADMIXTURE on them, and reads its
results back into a `gt_admix` object, with the log-likelihood and the log
of each run. With `conda_env = "auto"` (the default), it uses the ADMIXTURE
installed by `tgc_tools_install()`:

```{r}
anole_adm <- gt_admixture(anole_gt, k = 3, seed = 1)
summary(anole_adm)
```

# Running ADAMIXTURE

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = adamixture_available)
```

`gt_adamixture()` runs ADAMIXTURE, which combines a spectral initialisation
(SVD and ALS) with accelerated block relaxation (BR-QN), on a `gen_tibble` or
on a set of PLINK files. Like `gt_fastmixture()`, it sets the number of
cores with `threads` and cross-validation with `cv`, and by default it only
returns the Q matrices (set `no_freqs = FALSE` to also keep the P matrices).
ADAMIXTURE prints its progress, which we turn off with `verbose = FALSE`:

```{r}
anole_ada <- gt_adamixture(anole_gt, k = 3, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
summary(anole_ada)
```

# Comparing the results

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = all_available)
```

All four programs return `gt_admix` objects, which can be plotted with
`autoplot()`. The labels of the clusters are arbitrary, so we first match
the clusters of `gt_radmix()`, fastmixture and ADAMIXTURE to those of
ADMIXTURE, so that each cluster has the same colour in all the plots:

```{r}
# all permutations of 1:n
permutations <- function(n) {
  if (n == 1) {
    return(matrix(1))
  }
  sub <- permutations(n - 1)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    cbind(i, matrix(setdiff(seq_len(n), i)[sub], nrow = nrow(sub)))
  }))
}
# reorder the clusters of a gt_admix object with a single run, to best
# match those of the Q matrix q_ref
match_clusters <- function(adm, q_ref) {
  q <- unclass(adm$Q[[1]])
  perms <- permutations(ncol(q))
  diffs <- apply(perms, 1, function(x) sum(abs(q[, x] - q_ref)))
  best <- perms[which.min(diffs), ]
  adm$Q[[1]] <- q_matrix(q[, best])
  if (!is.null(adm$P)) {
    adm$P[[1]] <- adm$P[[1]][, best]
  }
  adm
}
q_adm <- unclass(anole_adm$Q[[1]])
anole_radmix <- match_clusters(anole_radmix, q_adm)
anole_fm <- match_clusters(anole_fm, q_adm)
anole_ada <- match_clusters(anole_ada, q_adm)
```

```{r, fig.height = 10.5}
library(ggplot2)
plots <- list(
  autoplot(anole_radmix, type = "barplot", k = 3, run = 1,
    annotate_group = TRUE
  ) +
    ggtitle("gt_radmix"),
  autoplot(anole_fm, type = "barplot", k = 3, run = 1,
    annotate_group = TRUE
  ) +
    ggtitle("fastmixture"),
  autoplot(anole_ada, type = "barplot", k = 3, run = 1,
    annotate_group = TRUE
  ) +
    ggtitle("ADAMIXTURE"),
  autoplot(anole_adm, type = "barplot", k = 3, run = 1,
    annotate_group = TRUE
  ) +
    ggtitle("ADMIXTURE")
)
patchwork::wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 1)
```

The four plots look the same. To confirm it, we compare the ancestry
proportions of each individual with those estimated by ADMIXTURE:

```{r}
q_differences <- function(adm) {
  q <- unclass(adm$Q[[1]])
  c(
    max_abs_difference = max(abs(q - q_adm)),
    correlation = stats::cor(as.vector(q), as.vector(q_adm))
  )
}
rbind(
  gt_radmix = q_differences(anole_radmix),
  fastmixture = q_differences(anole_fm),
  ADAMIXTURE = q_differences(anole_ada)
)
```

# Cross-validation

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

To choose K, all four programs can compute a cross-validation error for
each run, with `crossval = TRUE` in `gt_radmix()` and `gt_admixture()`, and
with `cv` (the number of folds) in `gt_fastmixture()` and
`gt_adamixture()`:

```{r}
gt_radmix(anole_gt, k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, crossval = TRUE)
gt_admixture(anole_gt, k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, crossval = TRUE)
gt_fastmixture(anole_gt, k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, cv = 5)
gt_adamixture(anole_gt, k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, cv = 5)
```

`gt_radmix()` implements the procedure of ADMIXTURE, which hides random
genotypes. ADAMIXTURE also hides random genotypes, but it refits each fold
with only 5 iterations, starting from the estimates of the full data.
fastmixture instead hides whole individuals. The errors of the programs are
therefore on different scales, and only the values of K that they favour
can be compared.

# References

Alexander DH, Novembre J, Lange K (2009) Fast model-based estimation of
ancestry in unrelated individuals. Genome Research, 19(9), 1655-1664.

Ko S, Chu BB, Peterson D, Okenwa C, Papp JC, Alexander DH, Sobel EM, Zhou H,
Lange KL (2023) Unsupervised discovery of ancestry informative markers and
genetic admixture proportions in biobank-scale datasets. The American
Journal of Human Genetics, 110(2), 314-325.

Prates I, Penna A, Rodrigues MT, Carnaval AC (2018) Local adaptation in
mainland anole lizards: Integrating population history and genome-environment
associations. Ecology and Evolution, 8(23), 11932-11944.

Saurina-i-Ricos J, Mas Montserrat D, Ioannidis AG (2026) ADAMIXTURE:
adaptive first-order optimization for biobank-scale genetic clustering.
Bioinformatics, 42(Supplement_1), btag236.
https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btag236

Santander CG, Refoyo Martinez A, Meisner J (2024) Faster model-based
estimation of ancestry proportions. Peer Community Journal, 4: e115.
https://doi.org/10.24072/pcjournal.503
